Balcony Waterproofing in Canberra for Leaks Into the Room Below

A stain below a balcony does not locate the water-entry point. Check connected details, drainage and the boundary between local sealing and membrane renewal.

Balcony waterproofing & leak repairs

We inspect the affected area, explain the appropriate repair work and confirm a written quote.

Request assessmentCall 0482 422 607

By MEL ONE · Updated 14 October 2026

Balcony leak planning

A ceiling stain beneath a balcony is a reason to investigate the whole water path before choosing a repair. Rain may be reaching a vulnerable balcony detail, gathering at an outlet or entering through an adjoining wall or door. The visible stain tells you where water became noticeable, not necessarily where it entered. This guide explains what to record, how a local repair differs from membrane renewal, and what an assessment and written scope should establish for a Canberra property.

Rain timing and ceiling leaks below a balcony

Start with the relationship between the weather and the leak. Record whether the room below becomes wet during the rain, several hours afterwards or only after repeated wet days. Note whether wind from a particular direction seems to matter. A leak after balcony washing is also worth recording, but do not recreate it deliberately. These observations help define an inspection; none proves that a membrane has failed.

Photograph the whole ceiling and a closer view of the affected patch. Include enough of the room to locate it later against the balcony above. Mark the date in your notes and say whether the stain is old, expanding or actively dripping. If water is near lights or electrical fittings, keep away from the affected area and arrange appropriate urgent assistance. Keep people clear of a sagging or visibly damaged ceiling.

Explain any recent work, including new tiles, a replaced sliding door, added planters or previous sealing. A change in when the leak occurs can be more useful than guessing which product will stop it.

Waterproofing repair distinctions

Selected distinctions from this guide
ConsiderationStarting point for assessment
Paving or elevated balconyGround-level paving and an elevated balcony over an occupied room need different investigations. Identify what lies below the outdoor surface.
Local sealingLocal sealing treats the specified joint or detail; it does not replace concealed waterproofing. Confirm the entry path and repair boundary.
Access through finishesTile removal depends on the confirmed cause, access and connection to the surrounding system. A surface photograph cannot confirm whether a repair without tile removal is feasible.

Read the linked sections to compare repair options, materials and preparation.

Balcony outlets, thresholds, edges and seams

A balcony assessment needs to look beyond the open tiled area. Relevant locations include the drain connection, door threshold, wall junctions, exposed edges, movement joints and penetrations for fittings. The assessor should identify the balcony construction and which details are accessible rather than treating every tiled deck as the same assembly.

ARDEX's technical bulletin for compressed fibre cement balconies illustrates this connection between falls, outlet detailing, door flashing, joints and the membrane. It is guidance for that particular construction, not a universal repair specification. Its balcony waterproofing bulletin provides a useful reference for why the floor cannot be considered in isolation.

From a safe position, note where water collects and whether leaves or objects cover an outlet. Report water reaching the door track or remaining in the same low spot after rain. Avoid reaching into concealed drains or removing fixed covers. The inspection should distinguish a surface obstruction from a drainage connection or level problem before a repair is selected.

The limits of leak stains and surface inspection

Drawing a straight line from a ceiling stain to the tile above it is tempting. Use that position as a starting point, then ask what evidence connects the two. An adjoining wall, door assembly or other external detail may also need review. If several entry paths remain plausible, the scope should describe the further investigation needed rather than present the first visible defect as a confirmed cause.

A photograph of cracked grout or split silicone can identify an item needing attention. It cannot show the condition of a concealed membrane or its connection to an outlet. Ask the assessor to separate visible findings, likely explanations and matters that remain unverified. This is especially useful when comparing a small resealing proposal with a more extensive renewal proposal.

Access to the room below can help relate the reported damage to the exterior layout. Any opening of finishes or controlled testing should be agreed in advance, including protection, access and reinstatement. Do not block a balcony drain and perform your own flood test above an occupied room.

Ground paving and balconies over occupied rooms

Describe what lies beneath the outdoor surface when you request help. A ground-level patio beside the house presents a different investigation from an elevated tiled balcony above a bedroom, office or living area. A search for balcony leak repairs can cover both situations, but the repair plan should not confuse them.

For ground paving, record water pooling against the building, the direction of runoff and any entry at the back door. That information belongs with an external waterproofing and drainage assessment. For a balcony over a room, include the ceiling symptoms, balcony layout and safe access to both levels.

Also identify whether the area is open to rain, partly covered or enclosed. Mention adjoining roofs, walls and neighbouring balconies without assuming they are responsible. The purpose is to give the assessor a usable description of the setting, not to settle a diagnosis before the property has been inspected.

Resealing and membrane renewal serve different purposes

Local sealing work addresses the specific joint or detail included in its scope. It should not be described as replacing a concealed waterproofing system. When a quote proposes resealing, ask which entry path it addresses, what preparation is included and what evidence supports limiting the work to that location.

Likewise, a proposal to renew waterproofing should explain what will be removed, what will be exposed and how the repaired area will connect with adjoining construction. ARDEX publishes a separate balcony edge detail, a reminder that even an edge is a designed part of a system.

Be cautious about treating a new grout colour or a fresh bead of silicone as proof that the source has been resolved. Ask for a clear explanation of the intended outcome and remaining uncertainty. If previous sealing has not stopped the same rain leak, provide that history so the next proposal can address the unresolved question rather than repeat the earlier scope without review.

Tile removal depends on the confirmed repair path

A balcony leak does not automatically mean every tile must be removed. Equally, a no-tile-removal repair cannot be promised from a photograph of the finished surface. The decision depends on the cause, access, existing construction and whether the required detail can be repaired with a suitable connection to the surrounding system.

For a local proposal, request the exact repair boundary and an explanation of how concealed conditions affect confidence in that approach. For an overlay proposal, ask which existing layers remain, what checks support their suitability and how door and drainage details will be handled. An overlay is a proposed construction method that needs assessment, not a general answer to all leaks.

Where removal is recommended, the quote should connect it to a purpose: exposing a concealed detail, preparing a sound surface or enabling the specified renewal. Ask how unexpected findings will be documented and approved. This makes the difference between initial investigation and confirmed construction work visible before disruption begins.

A written scope for balcony repair or renewal

Compare proposals by the water path and construction they address. A local repair is more understandable when a specific defect has been identified and the remaining assembly can support the proposed work. Broader renewal needs an explanation too, particularly when the assessment cannot establish a dependable local repair boundary.

The written scope should identify:

  • The balcony area, affected details and access arrangements.
  • Removal, preparation and any further investigation included.
  • Waterproofing, sealing, drainage interfaces and reinstatement work.
  • Separate trade tasks and the process for approving additional work.
  • Site protection, weather arrangements and checks before handover.

Keep ceiling repairs below the balcony visible in the discussion. Ask when those finishes can be assessed for reinstatement and who includes that work. A waterproofing quote and an interior restoration quote may cover different tasks. For balcony waterproofing and leak repairs, MEL ONE's Ellis team confirms the agreed work in the property-specific scope.

Balcony leak photos, access and property coordination

For an apartment, townhouse complex or managed commercial building, establish the authorised contact and required approvals before intrusive investigation or repairs. Arrange access to the affected room and balcony, and identify any shared areas needed for equipment or protection. This guide does not allocate strata responsibility or decide who pays; those questions depend on the property's arrangements and appropriate advice.

Send a small, useful photo set: the whole balcony, outlet, door threshold, visible damaged joints and ceiling below. Add the property type, Canberra or ACT address, leak timing and previous repair history. State any limits on access, business operations or use of the room underneath. Do not climb outside balustrades or onto adjoining roofs for photographs.

MEL ONE's Ellis team can use this information to prepare for an assessment across residential, strata and commercial properties in the ACT. The next step is to establish the source, accessible construction and practical scope. A clear record gives that discussion a firmer basis than choosing resealing or full renewal from the stain alone.

Related waterproofing questions

Can a balcony leak into the room below only during heavy rain?

Yes, a leak can be intermittent. Record the rainfall, wind, delay before dripping and any visible ponding. Heavy-rain timing helps direct an assessment, but does not by itself distinguish an outlet, threshold, wall detail or concealed membrane problem.

Can a leaking balcony be repaired without removing tiles?

Sometimes a defined, accessible defect may allow a local repair. Suitability depends on the confirmed water path, existing construction and the proposed repair connection. A concealed membrane problem or unsuitable underlying layers may require removal; a surface photograph cannot settle that choice.

What should I send before a balcony leak assessment?

Send safe photographs of the balcony, drain, threshold and damage below, plus the property address, rain timing and previous repairs. Identify the authorised property contact and access to both levels. Avoid deliberate flooding or opening finishes yourself.

Kitchen Sink Resealing and Plumbing Leak Assessment in Canberra

A wet cupboard can involve a sink joint, plumbing or an appliance. Confirm the source before resealing, then assess cabinet restoration separately.

Kitchen sealing & resealing

We inspect the affected area, explain the appropriate repair work and confirm a written quote.

Request assessmentCall 0482 422 607

By MEL ONE · Updated 14 October 2026

Kitchen leak planning

Water in the cupboard under a kitchen sink does not identify the failed part. An accessible sink-edge seal may need replacement, but a supply connection, waste fitting or appliance can leave water in the same cupboard. Start with the timing and first visible wet point, then agree an assessment that separates sealing from plumbing and cabinet restoration. We assess the affected detail on site and confirm the proposed work in writing.

Sink perimeter leaks and plumbing leak paths

A sink perimeter joint sits between the sink and benchtop. A splashback joint sits where the benchtop meets the wall finish. Either can let surface water reach an adjoining gap when the joint has failed. That is a different repair from a leaking tap connection, supply hose, waste assembly or pipe. A bead of silicone around the sink cannot repair those plumbing components.

Water can also travel along a surface before dripping. The lowest wet corner of the cupboard may be some distance from the starting point. Treat stains and pooled water as clues for inspection, rather than proof that the nearest joint needs sealing. Tell the assessor whether water follows bench cleaning, ordinary sink use, draining a full bowl or an appliance cycle. These patterns help organise the investigation; they do not establish a diagnosis by themselves.

For an accessible joint repair, the relevant service is kitchen sealing and resealing. A confirmed supply or waste fault needs plumbing assessment and its own repair scope.

Waterproofing repair distinctions

Selected distinctions from this guide
ConsiderationStarting point for assessment
Joints and plumbingSink-edge and splashback sealing treats accessible joints; it cannot repair a leaking tap, supply hose, waste assembly or pipe.
Cabinet restorationAddress the moisture source before cabinet restoration. Resealing cannot restore swollen, softened or delaminated board.
Sealant compatibilitySelect sealant for the actual sink, benchtop and splashback materials. Check preparation and product-specific curing before returning the joint to use.

Read the linked sections to compare repair options, materials and preparation.

Useful observations before a kitchen leak inspection

You can contact MEL ONE without photographs or measurements. If the area is safely accessible, a short description of the first place you noticed water is useful. Note whether the benchtop was wet, whether the tap or sink had recently been used, and whether the dishwasher or another connected appliance was operating. Existing photographs taken from a normal standing position can help explain the layout.

Keep observations passive. Do not deliberately flood the bench, fill the cupboard area, loosen fittings or pull an appliance out to reproduce a leak. Do not crawl into a damaged cabinet or reach near wet electrical fittings. If a leak is active, stop using the affected fixture where practical and arrange appropriate help. Active water near electricity needs prompt attention from the relevant professional.

A simple note such as “the cupboard was wet before breakfast, with no sink use since last night” gives more useful context than a guess about the membrane. Include earlier repairs and whether the wet patch is spreading.

Kitchen moisture appearing while the sink is unused

Water found while the sink is unused deserves a broader check than the visible sink edge. A water supply connection can remain pressurised when the tap is closed. An appliance may also run independently of sink use. Water remaining from an earlier event can take time to become visible, so an overnight wet patch does not prove a particular source.

Report when the cupboard was last seen dry, when you found the moisture, and whether nearby appliances were running. Distinguish fresh droplets you can already see from an old stain or swollen panel. Do not disconnect hoses, dismantle a trap or attempt isolation repairs to investigate. The person assessing the plumbing can decide what controlled checks are appropriate.

If the accessible perimeter looks intact but the cupboard keeps getting wet, adding more surface silicone may delay the correct repair. Ask for the suspected water path and the limits of the initial inspection to be explained before approving work.

Swollen cabinet repair after the moisture source is addressed

Resealing does not restore swollen, softened or delaminated cabinet board. It can address a confirmed joint leak, but the damaged material remains a separate issue. Replacing the board while the source is unresolved risks exposing the new material to the same water. Establish the leak path first, agree the repair, then assess what cabinet work is needed.

Tell the team whether a shelf has sagged, a door no longer closes, or a panel has pulled away from an adjoining surface. Avoid loading damaged shelves or disturbing a sink support. These observations help the assessor consider access and whether the surrounding construction can support the proposed repair.

Ask the written scope to distinguish source repair, any opening needed to reach it, drying or further condition checks, and cabinet restoration. A sealing quote should not imply that it includes replacing a cabinet carcass or remaking a benchtop unless those tasks are expressly listed. Keep photographs and the agreed scope together for later follow-up.

Split kitchen splashback silicone and recurring joint movement

A split at the splashback-to-benchtop junction is worth reporting even when the cupboard is dry. Note whether the sealant has separated from one edge, cracked through the bead or become detached in several places. The assessor needs to inspect the surfaces and joint, including any movement or damaged edges that could affect a replacement seal.

Painting over a split or spreading a new bead across loose material does not answer why the joint opened. The repair scope should identify removal of failed material, preparation of the exposed joint and the sealant suitable for its materials and movement. If a splashback or benchtop is loose, address that condition as part of the plan before treating the gap as a routine cosmetic repair.

Kitchen corners and sink edges are separate details. Ask which joints are included rather than assuming that “kitchen resealing” covers every junction in the room. A marked photograph or a written list can make the boundary clear.

Sealant compatibility, preparation and curing

Sealant choice depends on the actual benchtop, sink and splashback materials. Stone, laminate, metal and coated surfaces should not be treated as interchangeable. For example, Sika’s Sikasil-702 product information includes kitchen and splashback uses but excludes natural stone and certain other materials. A kitchen label alone does not establish compatibility with your installation.

Ask how the joint will be prepared and whether a manufacturer-specified pretreatment or a different product is needed. Sika’s guidance for that product calls for a sound, clean and dry substrate; primer is not a substitute for poor preparation. This is a product example, not a declaration that MEL ONE uses it on every kitchen.

Agree return-to-use instructions for the selected sealant. Sika’s curing guidance describes moisture curing and the influence of humidity and temperature. Surface skinning is not the same as full cure through a joint. Avoid assuming one fixed number of hours for every bead, product and Canberra season.

Domestic kitchen sealing and bathroom waterproofing requirements

The ABCB waterproofing FAQ excludes domestic food preparation areas from its wet-area definition. A residential kitchen therefore should not automatically receive the same waterproofing scope as a bathroom. This does not establish that a particular kitchen project has no requirements: its use, construction and applicable ACT rules still need checking.

For a sink-edge leak, ask for the actual junction work and any associated damage to be identified. For a wider renovation, describe changes to the floor, plumbing, cabinetry and adjoining areas before accepting a proposal. Do not use a bathroom membrane quotation as a template without checking whether the work addresses the kitchen’s confirmed problem.

The guide to regrouting, resealing and rewaterproofing explains the distinction between surface joint work and renewal of a concealed waterproofing system. Neither category replaces the need to find a plumbing leak.

A clear kitchen repair enquiry and written scope

Start with your Canberra or ACT address, the affected sink or junction and when moisture appears. Mention a swollen cupboard, previous sealing work and any appliance connection nearby. For a rented property, notify the property manager and agree who can authorise work. For strata property, identify any access or approval arrangements relevant to the affected area.

A useful scope names the joints to reseal, preparation and materials, plumbing tasks requiring separate attention, and whether cabinet repairs or reinstatement are included. If opening the area reveals more damage, ask for the finding, proposed extra work and its effect on cost and use of the kitchen before approving the change.

Arrange access to the sink and cupboard without dismantling anything yourself. Confirm when the repaired joint can be exposed to water and what to report if moisture returns. Describe your kitchen leak to MEL ONE; optional photographs can support the enquiry, and the on-site assessment establishes the repair plan.

Related waterproofing questions

Can sink resealing fix a wet cupboard?

It can address a confirmed leak through an accessible sink perimeter or adjoining joint. A leaking supply, waste or appliance connection needs its own assessment. The wet cupboard alone does not tell you which repair is suitable.

Should I replace a swollen cabinet board before finding the leak?

Find and address the moisture source before arranging restoration. Resealing does not reverse swelling or restore the strength of damaged board. Ask for source repair and cabinet restoration to be described separately.

Does a split splashback joint mean the kitchen needs bathroom-style waterproofing?

No. The joint and surrounding materials need assessment. Domestic kitchens are excluded from the NCC wet-area definition described in the ABCB FAQ, and the particular construction and ACT project requirements still need checking.

MEL ONE waterproofing guide

Shower Regrouting, Resealing and Rewaterproofing in Canberra

Grout, flexible sealant and the membrane serve separate roles. Compare the part being repaired before comparing surface treatments or renewal.

Shower resealing & regrouting

We inspect the affected area, explain the appropriate repair work and confirm a written quote.

Request assessmentCall 0482 422 607

By MEL ONE · Updated 14 October 2026

Shower repair planning

Regrouting, resealing and rewaterproofing work on different parts of a shower. A clean new joint may improve a worn finish, but the right repair depends on where water is escaping and what remains sound. This guide helps Canberra property owners compare the proposed work, understand epoxy grout and silicone, and recognise when a leak needs investigation before another surface treatment.

Three Shower Repair Options

Regrouting renews material between tiles within the agreed area. Resealing renews selected sealant joints, such as appropriate exposed junctions or screen interfaces. Rewaterproofing works on the waterproofing system, often with removal and reinstatement of finishes to obtain access. The words should not be used interchangeably in a quote.

Imagine three apparently similar showers. One has worn grout but no reported water escaping. Another sends water past a screen edge during use. A third causes dampness in an adjoining room despite recent surface repairs. The first needs a condition assessment of the finish; the second needs the escape route checked; the third needs the leak source reconsidered. Appearance alone cannot establish the concealed membrane condition in any of them.

Before comparing prices, make sure the proposed jobs address the same outcome. A quote to renew grout is not equivalent to a quote that removes tiles, repairs the substrate and reinstates waterproofing.

Waterproofing repair distinctions

Selected distinctions from this guide
ConsiderationStarting point for assessment
Repair scopesRegrouting renews tile joints, resealing renews selected sealant joints, and rewaterproofing reaches the underlying system, often through the finishes.
Material rolesGrout fills tile joints; silicone seals suitable flexible joints; the membrane is a separate waterproofing layer.
Grout selectionEpoxy and cement-based grout must suit the selected product and site. Grout choice does not resolve an unexplained pipe or membrane leak.

Read the linked sections to compare repair options, materials and preparation.

Grout, Silicone and Membrane Roles

Grout fills the joints within the tile finish. Silicone is a flexible sealant used at suitable joints. The membrane forms a separate waterproofing layer within the wet-area construction. Sika's sheet membrane system lists membrane, detailing components, adhesive and grout separately. That distinction matters when a surface repair is described as waterproofing.

A split sealant joint may allow unwanted water entry at that location. Replacing it does not inspect or reconstruct every concealed junction. Similarly, visible grout loss is a maintenance concern, but it does not prove that the underlying membrane has failed. The surrounding assembly and actual leak path still need assessment.

If a quote offers “full shower sealing”, ask exactly which joints and products it covers. Request a clear statement about whether the work is confined to the tile surface or includes the underlying waterproofing. The phrase alone tells you little about the investigation, access or construction being repaired.

Epoxy Grout and Cement-Based Grout

Epoxy and cement-based grouts are different product families, with suitability determined by the selected product and site conditions. ARDEX describes EG 15 epoxy grout for applications needing hygiene and chemical or physical resistance, and flags special procedures for some tile surfaces. A product's strengths do not make it a universal answer to an unexplained leak.

We provide epoxy grout work and check the existing tiles, joint condition and preparation before recommending it. Ask which product is proposed, why it suits the tile finish, and how residue and appearance will be managed. A useful comparison discusses the actual application rather than treating “epoxy” as a promise that any shower can be repaired from above.

If water continues to reach another room, the repair decision extends beyond grout selection. Epoxy in the tile joints cannot reconnect a leaking pipe or reconstruct an inaccessible membrane termination. Those possibilities must remain part of the assessment until the evidence supports a narrower scope.

Shower Movement Joints and Membrane Bond Breaker Details

Rigid tile joints and flexible junctions have different purposes. Where an exposed corner has repeatedly cracked or opened, a professional should check how the junction is intended to accommodate movement. Simply replacing the visible material with a harder product does not explain why the joint opened.

A bond breaker is a detail within a waterproofing system that allows the membrane to accommodate movement across a junction. It is not another name for the visible silicone bead on the finished tiles. ARDEX explains the purpose and different system approaches in its bond breaker guidance. Its SE sealant page also distinguishes sealant applications and the product specified beneath its membranes.

A photo of the finished corner cannot confirm that the concealed detail was installed correctly. If reconstruction is proposed, ask how the junction will be detailed as part of the chosen system. Avoid a generic instruction to put any silicone under any membrane; compatibility and the system specification matter.

Old Shower Silicone Removal and Sealant Joint Preparation

A thick new bead over loose or contaminated old silicone may make a joint look renewed while leaving the original adhesion problem unresolved. When sealant is peeling at an edge, the visible separation gives a location to inspect. It does not establish whether water has already affected the surrounding construction or whether sealing that joint will resolve the entire leak.

Ask what removal, cleaning and drying the proposed repair includes. Sika's sealant preparation guidance requires a sound, clean, dry surface free of contaminants, including old sealants. The Australian project still needs a suitable locally specified product and its own current instructions; that example is not a product recommendation for every shower.

Preparation should also account for fragile edges, existing damage and access. Removing material aggressively can disturb the finish or deeper layers. The service description should identify which joints are being renewed and what happens if removal reveals an unsuitable surface. These are practical scope questions for shower resealing and regrouting.

A Shower Still Leaking After Regrouting

A shower still leaking after regrouting needs a review of the diagnosis and the work completed. Record whether the symptom is identical, smaller, larger or in a new location. Note whether the shower was returned to use according to the repair instructions, and keep the product and scope information. A recurrence does not, by itself, prove either poor workmanship or membrane failure.

Possible explanations include a source outside the grouted joints, an unresolved junction, plumbing, or concealed waterproofing defects. Previously wet materials can also complicate interpretation of what is seen after a repair. An inspection should distinguish ongoing water entry from damage that has not yet been assessed or restored.

Pause use if it is causing further damage and have the relevant trade reassess the source. The plumbing and waterproofing leak guide explains useful observations. A further coating or another bead of sealant should have an explained purpose and defined boundary, rather than be the automatic response to a failed first attempt.

Partial Repair and Rewaterproofing Limits

A local repair may be appropriate when the defect and repair boundary are understood. For example, a confirmed exposed seal failure can justify a defined joint repair. However, a small area of visible damage is not proof that the required waterproofing repair can remain equally small. The condition of the substrate and the ability to connect to sound existing waterproofing may affect the scope.

Where tiles need removal, ask how access will be opened, which fixtures may be affected and what the proposal assumes about the remaining construction. A partial repair should explain the proposed connection to the retained system and the uncertainties that opening up may reveal. If that connection cannot be established, a wider scope may need consideration.

Rewaterproofing does not automatically mean renovating every part of the bathroom. Equally, keeping the work within the shower is an outcome to assess, not a promise to make from photographs. Bathroom waterproofing work should be scoped around the actual construction, access and restoration required.

Shower Grout and Sealant Curing with a Clear Handover

Return-to-use instructions depend on the products, application and conditions. A surface that feels dry is not a reliable substitute for the specified curing period. The ARDEX EG 15 data sheet distinguishes traffic and full-cure stages and notes temperature effects. Those figures belong to that product and stated conditions; they should not become a standard downtime promise for every repair.

Request written instructions identifying when the shower can be used and cleaned, and who to contact if water reappears. Where several products are involved, the handover needs to account for the whole repair sequence. Include any monitoring requested by the repairer, without deliberately stressing the shower or carrying out a home flood test.

Keep before-and-after photographs, the agreed scope, product details and findings together. For a cosmetic grout renewal, that records the finish work. For a leaking shower, it also preserves what was investigated and what remains outside the repair. Clear records help the next trade avoid repeating an assumption that the first job never established.

Related waterproofing questions

Does regrouting fix a leaking shower?

It may address a confirmed problem within the grouted finish, but it cannot be assumed to fix plumbing or concealed waterproofing defects. If water reaches another room or returns after regrouting, reassess the source before choosing another surface treatment.

Does silicone replace the waterproofing membrane?

No. Exposed silicone joints and the underlying waterproofing system have separate roles. Some systems specify compatible sealants within concealed details, but renewing the visible bead does not reconstruct or verify the membrane beneath the tiles.

Can epoxy grout avoid tile removal in every leaking shower?

No. Epoxy grout is a grout choice, not evidence that the hidden construction is sound. We provide epoxy grout work, with the repair scope determined by the defect, tile condition and preparation required. Some leaks need plumbing repairs or access to the waterproofing system.

A shower leak is a symptom, not a repair specification. Water beside an ensuite, behind a tiled wall or on the ceiling below can come from several parts of the bathroom. The useful first decision is which source needs investigation, rather than which surface needs more sealant. This guide explains how to record the pattern, protect the affected space and understand the limits of an initial assessment before choosing plumbing work, a local joint repair or rewaterproofing.

Plumbing, Surface Escape and Membrane Leaks

A bathroom has more than one route for water to escape. Supply pipework carries water to the shower fittings. The waste carries used water away. The screen and its joints help contain splash. Beneath the tile finish, the waterproofing system has its own connections, corners and terminations. A fault in one part does not establish the condition of the others.

For example, water visibly running under a screen door may explain a wet bathroom floor. It does not show whether a second leak exists beneath the tiles. Likewise, sound-looking grout cannot confirm that concealed waterproofing is intact. Sika describes an under-tile system that includes separate waterproofing, adhesive, grout and joint sealant stages in its bathroom guidance.

Use the initial description to request an investigation of the leak source. A plumber deals with pipework and waste faults; waterproofing and tiling work addresses the relevant building system. Some properties need both trades, with an agreed order of work.

Waterproofing repair distinctions

Selected distinctions from this guide
ConsiderationStarting point for assessment
Water pathsSupply and waste faults, escaping surface water and concealed membrane defects need different investigations and repair scopes.
Photographs and accessPhotos show visible joints and damage locations; they cannot establish concealed pipe, drain or membrane condition.
Repair boundariesA confirmed plumbing defect needs plumbing repair. Exposed joint work and access to concealed waterproofing are separate scopes.

Read the linked sections to compare repair options, materials and preparation.

Wet Carpet Next to a Shower

Wet carpet next to a shower deserves attention even when the bathroom itself looks dry. First record where the dampness starts: at the doorway, along the shared wall, around a pipe location or across a wider patch. A towel carried into the room, splash over a threshold, a screen leak or a concealed source can produce different patterns, but the visible wet edge alone cannot identify the route.

If the carpet repeatedly becomes wet after shower use, pause use of that shower and arrange assessment. Photograph the affected edge and the bathroom side of the same wall without lifting fixed finishes or disturbing damaged materials. Record whether the patch appeared immediately or was noticed later. That distinction helps the investigation; it does not prove a membrane failure.

A plumber may need to check supply and waste components before a waterproofing repair is specified. Carpet drying or replacement is a separate recovery task. Replacing the carpet before the source is addressed can hide the recurrence and leave the same uncertainty under a new finish.

Paint Bubbling on the Wall Behind a Shower

Paint bubbling on the wall behind a shower can be consistent with moisture reaching that wall, but paint failure is not a map of the leak. Condensation, an external water source, earlier damage and problems with the coating or wall surface may also need consideration. A bedroom wall that shares a boundary with a shower makes the bathroom relevant, not automatically responsible.

Take a wider photograph showing the wall and its position, followed by a closer image of the affected area. Note whether the skirting is also marked, whether the patch changes after shower use, and whether rain appears to influence it. Avoid repeatedly wetting the shower to demonstrate the problem. An inspection can plan any controlled testing that is justified.

Repainting is a finishing decision after the moisture source and the wall condition have been assessed. The waterproofer may need plumbing findings or access to concealed construction before recommending work. A painter cannot establish the integrity of a membrane merely by scraping the damaged paint.

A Ceiling Leak After the Upstairs Shower

Water dripping from a ceiling after an upstairs shower is used calls for stopping that shower and arranging prompt investigation. Keep people away from a visibly sagging ceiling and avoid contact with wet electrical fittings. Do not cut into the ceiling, remove a light fitting or stand beneath damaged material to collect a better photograph.

The source may involve the shower waste, a connection, water supply components, escaping surface water or waterproofing. Water can emerge somewhere other than the point where it first escaped, so a drip directly below the shower does not establish which layer has failed. Other fixtures nearby may also be relevant to the assessment.

Tell the person arranging access which room is above the mark and which fixtures were recently used. In an apartment or managed building, coordinate access to both affected spaces through the relevant property contact. Plumbing investigation and building repairs may need separate scopes. Ceiling restoration should follow source repair and assessment of the damaged materials, rather than conceal an unresolved leak.

Leak Timing as an Inspection Clue

The timing of a leak helps organise the investigation. Water noticed while a shower is unused may make supply pipework or another source relevant. A mark that appears during use can bring waste connections, splash containment and the wet-area construction into consideration. A delayed mark can reflect water travelling or remaining within the assembly. None of these patterns is a stand-alone diagnosis.

Prepare a short record from observations you already have:

  • The date, affected room and first place water was noticed.
  • Whether the shower had been used, and whether another nearby fixture was also in use.
  • Whether the symptom continued during a period when that shower was not used.
  • Any recent resealing, regrouting, plumbing work or change in the visible damage.

There is no need to reproduce the leak at home. Blocking a drain, flooding a floor or directing water into suspect joints can increase damage without isolating the source. Let the inspecting trade decide which checks are appropriate and how the results should be interpreted.

Shower Leak Photos and Non-Destructive Inspection Limits

Photos are useful for showing access, visible joints and damage location. They cannot show the complete membrane beneath tiles, the condition of a concealed pipe joint or whether every drain connection is sound. A neat bead of silicone is evidence of a visible finish, not proof of everything behind it.

A non-destructive inspection can narrow possibilities, but ask what was actually checked. If moisture readings or thermal images are used, ask what materials and conditions may influence them and what further evidence is needed. A reading or image should be interpreted with the building layout and other observations; it should not become a claim that every concealed defect has been found.

Some uncertainty remains until access is opened. The useful report separates observations, likely explanations and confirmed defects. It should explain why any proposed opening is needed, who will make it, what it may disturb and how reinstatement is handled. Declining unnecessary demolition does not require accepting an unsupported promise of a repair without tile removal.

Shower Leak Repairs Follow the Confirmed Defect

A confirmed pipe or waste defect needs the appropriate plumbing repair. A limited screen or exposed joint problem may suit a local repair after its condition and surrounding materials have been checked. Concealed membrane damage can require access through the finishes and a wider waterproofing scope. Those are different jobs, even if each began with the words “leaking shower”.

We explain the suspected leak source, the accessible checks and any further access needed before confirming the repair scope. If the work is limited to visible joints, the quote should make that boundary clear. The leaking shower repairs page explains the assessment route; bathroom waterproofing covers work involving the underlying wet-area system.

A persistent leak after resealing should trigger reassessment of the original explanation. Applying another surface product without understanding the result may repeat the same mismatch between symptom and repair.

A Useful Brief for a Shower Leak Inspection

For a Canberra or ACT property, send the Ellis team the address, property type, affected rooms, existing photographs and your observation record. Include any prior repair paperwork you have. For a rental or shared building, identify who can arrange access and approve investigation so the inspection does not depend on assumptions about another room or tenancy.

Request a written account of the findings and the next step, including any plumbing referral or further access needed. If rewaterproofing is proposed, ask which finishes and fixtures the scope includes. The ABCB notes that work to existing buildings depends on state and territory legislation; an online guide cannot settle the requirements for a particular alteration.

Keep the source investigation, repair decision and restoration record together. That makes the next decision easier if symptoms change and gives the relevant trades a shared account of what has already been observed and repaired.

Related waterproofing questions

Is my shower leaking from the plumbing or the waterproofing?

The visible symptom alone cannot reliably separate them. Record the location and timing, stop using a shower that is causing damage, and arrange investigation. Plumbing checks and a wet-area assessment may both be needed before the repair scope can be confirmed.

Does a dry bathroom floor rule out a shower leak?

No. A dry visible floor does not establish the condition of concealed pipework, waste connections or the waterproofing beneath finishes. It is one observation to include with photographs of the affected adjacent room or ceiling.

Can I send photos of wet carpet or bubbling paint from a suspected shower leak first?

Yes. Include a wide view, a close view and the position of the shower on the other side or above. Photos help explain the request and access needs, but they cannot confirm a concealed leak source or replace an on-site assessment.

Materials, sheet membranes and installation checks

Choose materials by location, substrate and exposure; understand sheet, PVC, TPO and polymer-cement systems before agreeing to the work.

Bathroom Waterproofing & Retiling · Balcony Waterproofing & Leak Repairs · Roof Waterproofing · Retaining Wall Waterproofing

Match the waterproofing system to the building part

For showers, bathrooms and laundries, consider a system documented for the wet-area substrate and intended tile or screed finish. Suitable liquid membranes and dedicated under-tile sheets are alternatives; neither product form is automatically right for every room.

A tiled balcony needs external under-tile suitability, drainage falls and continuous details at outlets, thresholds and wall junctions. An exposed roof needs a system designed for weather and UV exposure, with compatible terminations and the specified protection. A membrane designed to be covered is not automatically an exposed-roof finish.

Retaining walls need the water-pressure direction, access, drainage and protection before backfilling considered together. Permanent immersion, such as a pool or tank, needs explicit product and whole-system suitability. Pool and tank examples here explain material limits; they do not add a new MEL ONE service offering.

Sheet membranes: roofs, under tiles and below ground

Sheet describes a factory-made form, not one chemistry or one installation method. Modified bitumen, synthetic rubber, PVC and TPO sheets have different roles. ARDEX WPM 185 is a mineral-faced APP modified-bitumen cap sheet for exposed roof or deck systems; it is not a generic bathroom liner. Some bituminous sheets are torch-applied and others self-adhesive, so even the fixing method must be selected by model.

Dedicated under-tile sheets also exist. ARDEX WPM 750 is specified for internal tiled wet areas and uses heat-welded seams with selected compatible tiling systems. Other sheets can use different jointing methods. The quote should name the sheet, adhesive or fixing, seams, corners, penetrations and connection to the outlet rather than simply state “install a roll”.

PVC and TPO membranes need application-specific detailing

PVC is polyvinyl chloride; TPO is thermoplastic polyolefin, also described as FPO in some technical literature. They are different material families. Selected roofing sheets use hot-air-welded joints and an approved adhered, mechanically fixed or other specified roof build-up. Sarnafil G 410-20 L is one Australian PVC roofing example designed for direct exposure.

Below-ground PVC or FPO systems have their own arrangements for joints, terminations, protection and water pressure. The Sikaplan name covers different product ranges, including roofing and underground applications; the name alone does not establish the use. Confirm the precise model, substrate separation layers, compatibility and seam inspection method. Do not substitute a roof sheet for a shower or basement membrane because all are called PVC.

JS and polymer-modified cementitious waterproofing

In Chinese material descriptions, JS commonly refers to polymer-cement waterproofing coating. The useful Australian category is polymer-modified cementitious waterproofing, but that is a category comparison, not proof that two products are equivalent. A JS label or an overseas classification does not by itself establish suitability for an Australian wet area, balcony or basement.

Cementitious products can be flexible and can come in one- or two-component forms. Gripset C-1P is a one-component example for specified positive- and negative-pressure applications on suitable mineral substrates. Gripset 2P is a two-component example with documented under-tile, immersed and subterranean uses. Those permissions belong to the individual product: do not transfer them to every cement-based coating or every board substrate.

For a proposed cementitious system, confirm the substrate, movement demands, water-pressure direction, required thickness, curing and compatible covering. Use the supplied components and the nominated mixing procedure. Adding extra cement, water or an unrelated polymer changes the specified system.

Water-based and polyurethane liquid membranes

Water-based describes the carrier; polyurethane or acrylic describes chemistry. These categories can overlap: ARDEX WPM 155 Rapid Plus is a water-based polyurethane-acrylic hybrid intended for under-tile waterproofing. Gripset 38FC is a water-based SBR latex membrane used under specified coverings. The product data must establish outdoor use, covering requirements and substrate compatibility; “water-based” does not mean indoor-only.

Polyurethane is not automatically a complete UV-resistant roof system. Sikalastic-488 is a polyurethane base membrane; the SikaRoof MTC-12 UV system pairs it with a specified topcoat. An exposed-roof proposal must identify the complete build-up, any reinforcement, UV protection, permitted traffic and maintenance access. A product that tolerates rain is not necessarily suitable for permanent immersion.

Bitumen, epoxy and crystalline waterproofing systems

Liquid bitumen-rubber membranes differ from bituminous sheets. Gripset 51 is a liquid example for specified retaining-wall and underground uses; its documentation warns about long-term UV exposure. For a buried membrane, protection from backfill damage and the drainage design need separate attention. A coating does not correct structural movement or replace drainage work.

An epoxy barrier can have a different role from the flexible main membrane. ARDEX WPM 300 is an epoxy primer/barrier coating with specified moisture-control and pressure-resistant uses. It is not epoxy tile grout, and its role in a wet-area build-up must be identified rather than assumed. Xypex crystalline treatments work with suitable concrete; they are not a universal flexible covering for timber, board joints or moving cracks.

Waterproofing installation: checks before covering

ARDEX STB and STA illustrate the role of compatible detailing accessories: a butyl tape or sheet can form part of a nominated membrane junction system. It is not automatically a stand-alone membrane or an exposed finish. Check the specific membrane pairing rather than assuming any tape and liquid coating can be combined.

Assessment and preparation: establish the water source or new installation requirement, substrate stability, moisture condition and falls. Remove unsuitable coatings and repair the substrate as specified. Some systems require a dry base; others allow defined damp conditions. “Damp-compatible” does not mean application over flowing water or any wet surface.

Primer and details: use the specified primer where required. Complete the nominated corners, bond-breaker or joint-band arrangement, pipe collars, waterstops, outlets and terminations. A bond breaker is a movement detail within a system, not simply another name for the visible silicone joint. Follow the selected system rather than automatically adding the same tape and sealant everywhere.

Membrane installation: liquid systems need the specified coverage and wet/dry film thickness, without pinholes or unapproved thinning. Sheets need the specified support, adhesion or fixing, jointing and edge treatment. Hot-air welding, torch application and self-adhesive installation are different processes; require the appropriate installer, safety controls and system instructions. Do not use a generic welding temperature or lap dimension across products.

Curing, inspection and protection: distinguish recoat time, tiling time, testing time and return-to-service time. Temperature, humidity and the selected product affect these stages. Record membrane coverage or thickness checks and sheet-seam checks before covering. Any flood or other water test must suit the structure and system, occur after the required cure and be agreed in advance; it is not a DIY leak-finding exercise. Protect the finished membrane during tiling or backfilling.

Material selection and waterproofing quote records

A useful scope identifies the location and area, substrate preparation, brand and exact product, primer, main membrane, reinforcement or accessories, outlets and terminations, protection or tiling, and inspections. Record exclusions and separately required trades. A material name or “two coats” alone does not describe the installation quality or establish the finished thickness.

For Canberra projects, confirm the applicable NCC edition, ACT provisions and project approval with the responsible building professional. Domestic wet-area and external above-ground waterproofing have different requirements; a product test or overseas certificate alone does not certify the whole installation. Ask for the current Australian technical data, system instructions and relevant project records.

MEL ONE confirms the repair or installation scope for the inspected property. The products named here are educational examples, not a promise to use every brand or undertake every specialist installation. The selected system, suitability and any specialist work are confirmed for the job before approval.

Material and waterproofing system questions

Where are sheet waterproofing membranes used?

There are sheets for exposed roofs, internal under-tile wet areas and below-ground structures, but they are different systems. Select by exact product, substrate and exposure. For example, an APP roof cap sheet is different from a dedicated under-tile sheet. Seams, corners, outlets, fixing and protection are part of the specification; a roll of material alone is not a complete waterproofing system.

Can PVC or TPO roof membrane be used in a shower?

A roofing designation does not establish under-tile wet-area suitability. PVC and TPO are different material families, and roof, basement and under-tile products have different build-ups and joint details. Use a product explicitly documented for the intended wet-area substrate and tile finish, with its compatible adhesive and outlet details. The polymer name is not a substitute for the specific system instructions.

What does JS waterproofing mean in Australian product terms?

JS commonly describes polymer-cement coating in Chinese material terminology. The related Australian category is polymer-modified cementitious waterproofing; that is not a one-to-one product equivalence. Particular products can suit mineral walls, specified under-tile areas or immersion, and some allow negative-side pressure. Confirm the individual model and Australian documentation. A JS label alone does not prove bathroom, balcony or basement suitability.

Can a water-based waterproofing membrane be used outside?

Some products can, subject to their documented external use, substrate and covering requirements. Water-based describes the carrier, not the exposure rating. An external under-tile membrane may still need tiles or another specified cover and may not be suitable as an exposed roof finish. Confirm UV exposure, ponding, immersion and traffic separately rather than assuming all outdoor conditions are equivalent.

Does polyurethane waterproofing need a UV-resistant topcoat?

It depends on the exact product and complete exposed-roof system. Some polyurethane base membranes require a specified protective topcoat; others have different exposure instructions. Sikalastic-488 and the SikaRoof MTC-12 UV build-up illustrate why the base membrane and the whole system must be distinguished. Confirm the nominated layers and maintenance requirements instead of treating every PU coating as a finished roof surface.

Is an epoxy moisture barrier the main flexible waterproofing membrane?

Not automatically. A product such as ARDEX WPM 300 has specified primer and barrier roles, including certain moisture and pressure conditions. Its position in the selected build-up needs to be stated. It is different from epoxy tile grout and does not automatically replace the flexible membrane, joint detailing or compatible tiling system required for the wet area.

Does two coats prove the correct waterproofing thickness?

Coat count alone is not enough. Liquid membranes have product-specific coverage and wet or dry film requirements, together with preparation, detailing and cure conditions. A sheet has a manufactured thickness, but its seams and terminations still need the specified installation and checks. The quote and records should identify the selected system and relevant checks, not a universal number of coats or drying hours.

Can balcony waterproofing be used for a pool or retaining wall?

Only if that exact product and system document the proposed use. Permanent immersion and positive- or negative-side water pressure are different from ordinary balcony exposure. Below-ground work also needs suitable protection and drainage arrangements. Some cementitious or sheet systems have these uses, but the permissions cannot be transferred to every product in the same family. These examples do not confirm a pool installation service.

Manufacturer documentation for waterproofing materials

Manufacturer examples reviewed for this guide: ARDEX WPM 155 Rapid Plus, WPM 185, WPM 750 and WPM 300; Gripset 38FC, C-1P, 2P and 51; Sika Sarnafil G 410-20 L, Sikaplan ranges, Sikalastic-488 and SikaRoof MTC-12 UV; Xypex concrete treatments. Check the current Australian data for the exact proposed system.

The terminology comparison also considers Chinese manufacturer descriptions of polymer-cement (JS) coatings. ACT building-code adoption information and Australian wet-area guidance are regulatory context, not approval of a particular product or job.

MEL ONE waterproofing guide

External Waterproofing and Drainage Assessment in Canberra

Drainage manages where water goes; waterproofing addresses defined entry details. Record the moisture pattern before choosing a drain, coating or joint repair.

External waterproofing & water ingress repairs · Retaining wall waterproofing

We inspect the affected area, explain the appropriate repair work and confirm a written quote.

Request assessmentCall 0482 422 607

By MEL ONE · Updated 14 October 2026

External moisture assessment

Water beside a building and water entering a building are related observations, but they do not automatically require the same repair. Drainage work manages where water goes; waterproofing and sealing work address defined water-entry details. Some properties need both. Before choosing a coating, new drain or joint repair, establish when the moisture appears, where water gathers and which part of the building is affected. This guide helps Canberra owners and managers prepare that assessment without assuming every damp patch has the same cause.

The moisture pattern comes before the repair method

Describe the symptom in ordinary terms. Examples include a puddle against the wall after rain, a wet window reveal during windy weather, water crossing the back-door sill or dampness in a garage beside retained soil. These descriptions are useful because they locate the issue without naming an unconfirmed defect.

Record the first point at which you notice water and the time it appears. Distinguish active water from an old stain and note whether the surface dries between events. Include recent changes such as paving, landscaping, a door replacement or work to a nearby downpipe. An inspection can then compare the account with accessible building and site details.

Keep an open diagnosis where the evidence is incomplete. A wet wall after rain does not establish that the whole wall needs coating. A puddle near a door does not prove the door itself is defective. Ask for the findings, proposed cause and any uncertainty to be stated separately before agreeing to a construction method.

Waterproofing repair distinctions

Selected distinctions from this guide
ConsiderationStarting point for assessment
Pooling beside a wallA drainage proposal needs a collection point, route and suitable discharge destination. A channel beside the wall is incomplete without its discharge.
Wind-driven rainDistinguish the window assembly, accessible perimeter joint and adjoining wall or flashing before choosing sealing work.
Coordinated repair scopeDrainage manages collection and discharge. Waterproofing names the building detail, access and preparation; agree the interfaces and separate trade tasks.

Read the linked sections to compare repair options, materials and preparation.

Water pooling and wall-base moisture

For water pooling beside the house, observe the wider route rather than only the puddle. From a safe location, note whether runoff seems to arrive from paving, a garden, a downpipe area or higher ground. Photograph the surrounding layout and any visible drain, then take a closer image of the wall base. Say how long the water remains after the rain stops.

This is information for an assessment, not an instruction to redirect water yourself. A proposed drainage change needs a suitable discharge route and consideration of the whole site. Ask the responsible drainage trade to explain the collection point, route and destination. A new channel alongside the wall is not a complete proposal if its discharge has not been established.

If paving or soil has recently been raised, identify that change in the enquiry. Do not excavate along the footing or remove ground against a wall to expose a suspected membrane. The inspection should establish what access is safe and whether drainage, building details or both require further investigation.

Window leaks during wind-driven rain

For a window that leaks only with rain from one direction, record the room, affected side and first visible wet point. Include photographs of the whole window and the interior reveal. Exterior photographs should be taken only from normal, safe access. Mention whether water appears around the frame, at the sill or higher on the wall.

The assessment should consider the window assembly and its connection to the surrounding wall. Ask whether the proposed work concerns an accessible perimeter joint, a flashing detail, the window itself or another part of the facade. That distinction determines who needs to inspect and what a sealing quote can reasonably include.

A blanket instruction to seal every opening is not a useful substitute for identifying the assembly. Tell the contractor about earlier attempts and request an explanation of which joints are to be repaired. Avoid applying sealant to unfamiliar slots or drainage openings. Where the cause remains concealed, agree the investigation and reinstatement scope before finishes are opened.

Back-door rainwater leaks and adjoining paving

Water at a back door deserves a view of both sides of the threshold. Record whether you see runoff approaching the opening, water sitting outside the sill or moisture first appearing inside the frame. Note whether the door was closed and whether wind seemed to drive rain towards it. These details help distinguish the reported event without prescribing a repair.

Ground-level paving beside a door is different from a balcony above an occupied room. The former may require review of site runoff and threshold details. The latter also needs consideration of the construction over the room below; see the balcony leak guide for that situation.

Ask how any proposed paving, drainage or threshold change will connect with the existing door and wall. If more than one trade is involved, identify the sequence and handover between them. The objective is a coordinated scope for the reported entry path, including the finishes that must be removed and restored to reach it.

Condensation, rain entry and persistent low-level damp

Not all indoor moisture arrives as liquid rain. The Australian Government's YourHome condensation guidance explains that condensation forms when humid air meets a cooler surface and can occur both visibly and within construction. A rain-entry repair therefore needs evidence that it addresses the reported source.

Record whether droplets appear on glass on dry mornings, whether moisture follows cooking or showering, and whether the problem also occurs without rain. These clues can prompt assessment of ventilation or building conditions. They do not rule out a separate leak: more than one issue can exist at a property.

Persistent dampness low on a wall also needs a careful description. Staining, salts or peeling paint alone are not enough for this guide to diagnose rising damp, groundwater or a failed barrier. YourHome's repairs and maintenance guidance identifies several possible moisture sources. Ask the assessor what evidence supports the diagnosis and whether additional building, plumbing or moisture investigation is needed before selecting treatment.

Drainage and waterproofing in the same repair plan

A useful proposal gives each task a purpose. Drainage work should describe the water it will collect or redirect and the intended discharge arrangement. Waterproofing or sealing work should identify the part of the building it treats, the access and preparation needed, and the detail it is intended to protect. Avoid comparing proposals solely by the area of coating or length of drain.

Sika Australia's waterproofing guidance treats system selection, substrate preparation and falls to drainage as distinct considerations. Manufacturer information supports planning around the assembly and conditions; it does not establish which product is suitable for an unseen property.

Where both types of work are proposed, ask who resolves the interfaces. A drain installed beside a wall and a waterproofed wall detail must be considered together in the agreed design. The external waterproofing service scope should identify the Ellis team's work and any separate drainage task so the owner can see how the overall repair will be completed.

Retaining walls and adjoining garage moisture

A garage wall beside retained soil needs more context than an exposed external wall. Tell the assessor which side retains ground, what access exists outside and where moisture first appears inside. Include available plans and previous work records. If the soil-facing side cannot be reached, state that early; access can materially affect the investigation and possible scope.

Do not assume an internal coating is equivalent to repairing the retained side. Ask the proposal to explain the chosen repair side, the intended outcome and any unresolved drainage or access issue. Retaining wall waterproofing needs a defined area and method, with excavation, drainage and protection work identified where relevant.

This guide cannot assess wall stability or diagnose structural movement. Report visible changes such as a newly opening crack, displaced finish or apparent movement, and arrange appropriate specialist assessment. Do not dig behind a retaining wall, remove supporting soil or drill investigation holes yourself. Structural questions should be resolved by the relevant specialist before relying on a waterproofing-only proposal.

External leak observations and coordinated waterproofing scope

Prepare a short record that another person can follow: the ACT address, property type, affected room or exterior area, weather timing, photographs and previous repairs. Include one wide photograph to show the layout rather than sending only close-ups of damp paint. Observe rain from shelter where practical; avoid roofs, ladders, flooded areas and unstable ground.

For managed residential or commercial property, identify the authorised contact, tenant access and any operating restrictions. Agree what the first visit covers and what additional investigation would require separate approval. Plumbing, roofing, window, drainage, waterproofing and structural tasks may need different input. Each task should have an identified owner, sequence and reinstatement allowance.

MEL ONE's Ellis team assesses external water-ingress work across Canberra and the ACT for residential, strata and commercial properties. Request a written scope that connects the evidence to the proposed work, lists separate trade requirements and explains how unexpected findings will be handled. That gives you a practical basis for choosing the repair and coordinating access.

Related waterproofing questions

Does water pooling beside my house mean I need waterproofing?

Not automatically. The assessment should establish where the water comes from, where it can discharge and whether it is entering a building detail. The scope may require drainage, waterproofing or coordinated work by different trades.

Why does my window leak only in windy rain?

The weather pattern is useful evidence, but does not identify the defect on its own. Record the direction of the rain and the first visible wet point. An assessment should distinguish the window assembly, perimeter joint and adjoining wall or flashing details before proposing sealing.

Can I waterproof a damp garage retaining wall from the inside?

The repair side and method depend on the wall construction, water path and available access. An internal treatment should not be assumed to address retained-side drainage or structural issues. Ask for the intended outcome, limitations and separate specialist tasks to be explained in the scope.
